title: The Living Voice
subtitle: From the surviving fragments of his five books
source: Papias's five books, Expositions of the Oracles of the Lord, are lost. The fragments here are as Eusebius keeps them, Church History III.39, in the public-domain English of NPNF Series II Vol. 1 (1890), and as Irenaeus gives them, Against Heresies V.33, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 1 (1885). Editorial framing by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: A hearer of the elders
sections.framing: Papias was bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia, the same town where, two generations earlier, the Apostle Philip had been crucified. Irenaeus, as Eusebius quotes him, calls him “an ancient man who was a hearer of John and a companion of Polycarp.” He wrote, somewhere between 110 and 130, a five-volume work in Greek under the title Expositions of the Oracles of the Lord. The work is lost, but fragments large and small were preserved by Eusebius and Irenaeus, and through them the Church possesses some of the earliest reflections on the Gospels outside the New Testament.
paragraphs: If, then, any one came, who had been a follower of the elders, I questioned him in regard to the words of the elders,—what Andrew or what Peter said, or what was said by Philip, or by Thomas, or by James, or by John, or by Matthew, or by any other of the disciples of the Lord, and what things Aristion and the presbyter John, the disciples of the Lord, say. For I did not think that what was to be gotten from the books would profit me as much as what came from the living and abiding voice.
notes: Eusebius keeps Papias's preface in his Church History III.39. Its last words, “the living and abiding voice,” are the apostles' testimony as it passed from mouth to mouth before it was written down.

sections.title: What Matthew and Mark did
sections.framing: Two of the fragments preserved by Eusebius from Papias are the earliest external accounts of the writing of the Gospels of Matthew and Mark. They are short and matter-of-fact, and they have weighed in every patristic and modern discussion of the Gospels since.
paragraphs: This also the presbyter said: Mark, having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately, though not in order, whatsoever he remembered of the things said or done by Christ. For he neither heard the Lord nor followed him, but afterward, as I said, he followed Peter, who adapted his teaching to the needs of his hearers, but with no intention of giving a connected account of the Lord’s discourses, so that Mark committed no error while he thus wrote some things as he remembered them. For he was careful of one thing, not to omit any of the things which he had heard, and not to state any of them falsely.
So then Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language, and every one interpreted them as he was able.
notes: Papias's note that Mark wrote 'not in order' has been read in various ways: that Mark did not arrange his material chronologically, that he did not arrange it rhetorically, or that he wrote down what he heard without imposing a literary plan. The witness of the apostolic age does not press the question further.

sections.title: The blessed kingdom
sections.framing: In the fourth of his five books, Irenaeus tells us, Papias set down what the elders who had seen John said they had heard from him of the Lord's teaching on the age to come. The fragments are vivid and have been read in different ways: as a literal millenarianism, as a parable in the mode of the prophet Isaiah, or as a piece of Jewish-Christian piety. The Orthodox tradition has not received them dogmatically but keeps them as the witness of one of the earliest hearers.
paragraphs: The days will come, in which vines shall grow, each having ten thousand branches, and in each branch ten thousand twigs, and in each true twig ten thousand shoots, and in each one of the shoots ten thousand clusters, and on every one of the clusters ten thousand grapes, and every grape when pressed will give five and twenty metretes of wine. And when any one of the saints shall lay hold of a cluster, another shall cry out, “I am a better cluster, take me; bless the Lord through me.”
And these things are borne witness to in writing by Papias, the hearer of John, and a companion of Polycarp, in his fourth book; for there were five books compiled (συντεταγμένα) by him.
notes: Irenaeus quotes the saying in Against Heresies V.33.3 and attributes it through Papias to John, who in turn had it from the Lord. The image takes up the language of the prophet Amos and the apocryphal apocalypse of Baruch, and is in the spirit of Isaiah 25, the mountain of fat things and wines on the lees.
His memory is kept on the twenty-second of February, the day before his fellow-disciple Polycarp.
